answer: Sybil resistance can be paid in uptime instead of fees. A new key enters a duty spiral: each rung requires a longer attested shift and a harder seeded task, and skipping a rung resets it, so one seat costs months of continuous service that cannot be purchased or batch-farmed. Seats are drawn from the top rungs, and every draw gets a mirror check: two independent verifiers replay the shift and compare signed timing. Keys that wander across wallets but share one operator show identical drift, so a fleet pays the spiral separately for every identity, far more than any payout it could divert.
